# RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews the literature on which the study builds and outlines the gaps addressed by the research questions. The discussion begins with NLP of disaster posts and the lack of annotated resources for Taglish, followed by multi-task learning, negative transfer, and multi-task optimizers. The chapter concludes with a taxonomy matrix comparing key studies and a synthesis of the literature.

## Natural Language Processing of Disaster Posts

Crisis informatics has built most of its resources from English text annotated with categories for whole posts. Of the new text corpora found in a review of studies from 2020 to 2024, 47 of 89 were in English only, and only 7 of 91 were annotated with entities, relations, or events [@lewis2025tapping]. The main datasets for the two tasks of this study follow this pattern. HumAID annotated 77,196 English posts from 19 disasters with humanitarian categories [@alam2021humaid], and HUMAID-NER added entity annotations to 60,000 HumAID posts, so that the same posts are annotated for both tasks [@ali2026humaidner].

Philippine studies have used local disaster posts, but each trained a model for a single task, such as classifying posts as urgent [@ermino2022urgency] or informative [@somido2023actionable], or finding the locations affected by a volcanic eruption [@yute2021satellite]. The only Philippine system found in this review that both classifies messages and extracts their details sends each comment to GPT, a commercial LLM, instead of training a model, and it was tested only on simulated comments [@caoile2025urdaneta]. However, smaller pretrained models fine-tuned on annotated data have outperformed LLMs used zero-shot in general text classification [@bucher2024finetuned], the classification of crisis posts [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot], and Tagalog NER [@miranda2023tlunifiedner].

No dataset found in this review annotates the same Taglish posts for both humanitarian classification and NER, since HUMAID-NER, the only one with both on the same posts, is in English [@ali2026humaidner]. Even @zou2025typhoon, who trained one model for both tasks on Chinese typhoon posts, took the place names from an existing NER dataset rather than annotating the same posts for both. The gap reflects a wider shortage. Code-switching between Tagalog and English, known as Taglish, is extremely common in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish], yet Filipino lacks many of the datasets, tools, and pretrained models available for English [@cruz2022tagalog], and the Tagalog NER datasets that exist come from news, Wikipedia, historical newspapers, and posts on other topics rather than from disaster posts [@miranda2023tlunifiedner; @ramos2023tfnerd; @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner].

## Multi-Task Learning

Multi-task learning trains one model on several related tasks so that what the model learns for one task can help it learn the others, a process known as inductive transfer [@caruana1997multitask]. A popular design is hard parameter sharing, in which the tasks share one encoder and each task has its own task head [@vandenhende2022dense; @khanal2021location; @lin2023libmtl]. The tasks that share an encoder do not have to work on the same unit of text. Humanitarian classification assigns one category to a whole post, while NER makes a prediction for every token [@ali2026humaidner]. Sharing an encoder can also lower cost. A multi-task model computes the shared layers once for all tasks, which reduces memory and speeds up prediction [@vandenhende2022dense; @lin2023libmtl]. In training, it needs more computation for each update but often less in total than training each task separately [@caruana1997multitask]. Disaster studies have argued for these savings [@wang2021transformer; @ali2026humaidner] but did not measure them.

Sharing an encoder can, however, hurt a task, a problem known as negative transfer [@vandenhende2022dense; @royer2023scalarization], and its causes are debated. The usual explanation concerns the task gradients, the directions in which each task pushes the shared encoder to change during training. These gradients may conflict, so that a change that helps one task harms the other, or one may be much larger than the other and dominate the change [@yu2020pcgrad; @gama2026uniform]. The link to performance, however, is not direct. @royer2023scalarization found conflicting gradients throughout training, but low levels of conflict did not track performance. For NER and classification, @zhu2025prefinetuning traced the conflict to opposite demands on token representations, since NER makes entities of the same type more similar while classification makes the tokens of a text more uniform. PCGrad, a multi-task optimizer, recovered only 0.1 points on NER, while adding small modules for each task to the last two layers of the encoder removed the resulting drop in performance.

On disaster posts, training a whole-post task together with a token-level task has given mixed results. On Chinese typhoon posts, plain multi-task training changed the F1-score from 0.854 to 0.860 for place names and from 0.876 to 0.875 for damage types [@zou2025typhoon]. On English crisis posts, training location identification with three other tasks improved it in most settings, although the other tasks were not reported [@khanal2021location]. With fixed task weights, @ali2026humaidner found that classification on English disaster posts declined after the third epoch while NER kept improving, which they attributed to the much larger number of training signals from NER. None of these studies used Taglish, and none compared more than two multi-task optimizers.

A multi-task optimizer controls how the training signals of the tasks are combined into one update of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. The simplest optimizers keep the task weights fixed. Equal weighting gives the tasks the same weight [@kurin2022unitary], and linear scalarization keeps fixed weights chosen by trying several weight settings [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization]. The other optimizers are the SMTOs [@gama2026uniform], which either change the task weights during training based on the losses or combine the separate gradients of the tasks [@lin2022rlw; @lin2023libmtl]. @tbl-optimizers lists the 13 optimizers compared in this study, which come from seven studies that compared multi-task optimizers (Section 3.2).

| Optimizer | Family | How It Balances the Two Tasks |
|:------------------|:-----------|:----------------------------------------|
| Equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with the same weight |
| Linear scalarization [@xin2022mtohelp] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with fixed weights chosen by trying several settings |
| Random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw] | Loss | Draws new task weights at random at every update |
| Uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss | Gives less weight to the task whose predictions are more uncertain |
| DWA [@liu2019mtan] | Loss | Gives more weight to the task whose loss is falling more slowly |
| GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm] | Gradient | Adjusts the task weights so that both tasks learn at a similar speed |
| MGDA [@sener2018mgda] | Gradient | Combines the task gradients into the smallest update that improves both tasks |
| PCGrad [@yu2020pcgrad] | Gradient | When the task gradients conflict, removes the part of each that works against the other |
| GradDrop [@chen2020graddrop] | Gradient | Where the task gradients disagree in sign, keeps one sign chosen at random |
| IMTL [@liu2021imtl] | Loss and gradient | Scales the task gradients so that the update favors neither task, and keeps the losses at a similar size |
| GradVac [@wang2021gradvac] | Gradient | Adjusts the task gradients toward a target similarity tracked during training |
| CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] | Gradient | Finds an update close to the average of the task gradients that most helps the task gaining least |
| Nash-MTL [@navon2022bargaining] | Gradient | Treats the tasks as players that bargain over the shared update |

: Multi-Task Optimizers {#tbl-optimizers tbl-colwidths="[24,14,62]"}

Studies disagree on whether SMTOs perform better than fixed task weights. Five comparisons found little or no advantage. In @vandenhende2022dense, fixed weights chosen by a grid search outperformed nearly all the automated methods, and in @xin2022mtohelp and @royer2023scalarization, linear scalarization matched or outperformed the SMTOs. @xin2022mtohelp also found that tuning the training settings mattered more than the choice of optimizer. With regularization, equal weighting performed as well as the SMTOs in @kurin2022unitary, and random weights performed comparably in @lin2022rlw, who proposed random weighting as a litmus test for new optimizers. @gama2026uniform, however, found that SMTOs outperformed equal weighting on more complex problems, while on two similar tasks they learned weights close to equal and matched it. These comparisons used images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text, and none used disaster posts or Taglish. Since the optimizers act on the losses and gradients rather than on the text itself, they can be applied to posts in any language, as @xin2022mtohelp did across images and translation, but how well they work depends on the problem [@gama2026uniform].

The optimizers also differ in training cost. Optimizers that combine the gradients of the tasks must compute a separate gradient for each task, which takes extra time and memory, although this cost can be reduced by computing the gradients only at the output of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. Computing a gradient for each task lowered training speed from about 12 to about 5 updates per second in @xin2022mtohelp, and the SMTOs took longer per epoch than equal weighting in @kurin2022unitary. @royer2023scalarization questioned whether removing conflicts at every step justifies its extra computation and memory. Such costs matter because they make deep learning research harder for those with fewer computing resources [@schwartz2020green], yet none of the multi-task disaster studies reviewed here reported training time or memory.

|:---------|:---------------------|:-----------------------|:------------------|:------------------------|

| @wang2021transformer | BERT and other encoders shared by two task heads, with equal weighting | TREC Incident Streams English crisis posts, 6,658 test posts from 15 events | Information type F1, priority scores, ranking (NDCG), harmonic mean | English only, whole-post tasks only, equal weighting only, no training time or memory reported |

| @zou2025typhoon | Chinese BERT-base shared by a place-name head and a damage head, with fixed loss weights | 6,000 MSRA NER texts for place names, 6,000 Weibo typhoon posts for damage types | Precision, recall, and F1 for both tasks | Chinese only, tasks trained on different datasets, fixed weights only, no training time or memory reported |

| Somido and Reyes [-@somido2023actionable] | Logistic regression on word counts, word weights, and word vectors | 5,000 posts from five Philippine disasters in CrisisLexT26 | Accuracy, precision, recall, area under the curve, F-score | One binary task |

| @kurin2022unitary | Equal weighting compared with MGDA, IMTL, PCGrad, GradDrop, and random loss weighting | Multi-MNIST, CelebA, Cityscapes, Meta-World robot tasks | Accuracy, success rate, training time per epoch | Image and robot tasks only |

| @lin2023libmtl | LibMTL library with 13 optimizers and 8 architectures | NYUv2 | Task scores | Images only |

| Gama and Grassi [-@gama2026uniform] | Equal weighting compared with 14 SMTOs | Multi-MNIST, Cityscapes, QM9 molecules | Task scores, average change against single-task models | Images and molecules only |

As @tbl-matrix shows, no earlier study combines Taglish posts, both tasks annotated on the same posts, several multi-task optimizers, and measured training cost.

## Synthesis of Related Literature and Studies

The reviewed studies show three trends. First, datasets and models for disaster posts have been built mostly from English text, and the Philippine studies trained a model for one task or relied on a commercial LLM [@lewis2025tapping; @ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @yute2021satellite; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Second, training classification together with a token-level task such as NER has given mixed results [@zou2025typhoon; @khanal2021location; @ali2026humaidner], and one study traced negative transfer between the two to conflicting demands on the shared encoder [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. Third, studies disagree on whether SMTOs outperform fixed task weights, and their comparisons used images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text rather than disaster posts [@vandenhende2022dense; @xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @lin2022rlw; @royer2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform].

These trends leave two gaps. The first is the lack of a dataset in which the same Taglish posts are annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. The only dataset found with both kinds of annotation on the same posts is in English [@ali2026humaidner], and Taglish and Filipino have few annotated resources [@herrera2022tweettaglish; @cruz2022tagalog]. The first and second research questions address this gap. The study builds such a dataset, designs a multi-task model for it, and measures how well single-task models perform on it as the baseline.

The second gap is the lack of a comparison of multi-task optimizers for these two tasks on Taglish posts, in either negative transfer or training cost. None of the multi-task disaster studies compared more than two optimizers or reported training time or memory, and because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], results from other kinds of data cannot settle the choice for these posts. The third research question therefore compares the 13 optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory, and the fourth compares the final model, trained with the optimizer selected based on negative transfer, with the single-task models. Equal weighting serves as the reference in the third question, because several of the reviewed comparisons found that SMTOs did not outperform it.
